Book: Materialist Tendencies in Arab-Islamic Philosophy (Volume I)

Anyone with an interest in culture will know the historical and intellectual importance of the publication of the late scholar Husayn Muruwwa’s Materialist Tendencies in Arab-Islamic Philosophy. They will also know the gap this book filled in the Arabic library. Muruwwa intended it to be an encyclopedic work. It became especially important to democratic and progressive readers and institutions, as well as to individual intellectuals in general and progressive intellectuals in particular, not to mention university students and everyone with a broader interest in culture.
The problem was that this very large book was originally published by Dār al-Fārābī in only two volumes. The first ran to more than a thousand pages, while the second was around eight hundred pages.

Edition followed edition, and the book became an essential reference for intellectuals, university researchers, and students across the Arab world. Today, however, many readers may be interested in only one part of it. One may be concerned mainly with pre-Islamic Arabia, another only with questions of method, and another with the materialist analysis of Ibn Sīnā’s philosophy, regardless of the other sections. Buying only the part one needs also costs less than buying the whole work.
For these reasons, we decided to issue a new edition in four volumes:
Volume I: the book’s methodological introduction, followed by studies of pre-Islamic Arabia and the rise and early period of Islam.
Volume II: kalām, or Islamic theology, especially the Muʿtazila and Ashʿarism, followed by Aristotelian formal logic, since the Muʿtazila were the first to make use of it.

Volume III: Sufism, represented through only two examples, Ibn ʿArabī and al-Suhrawardī; the Epistles of the Brethren of Purity; and a short account of the development of the sciences among the Arabs.
Volume IV: the mature stage of philosophy: al-Kindī, al-Fārābī, and Ibn Sīnā.

Arab-Islamic thought in the Middle Ages: its distinctive features and historical role
This book presents a way of approaching the Arab-Islamic intellectual heritage based on a scientific method that Arab authors have only recently begun to use.

From the Middle Ages, when this intellectual heritage took shape in its many forms, down to our own time, most studies of it have shared the same basic weakness. Despite the differences between their schools and tendencies, they have generally looked at the intellectual achievements of the medieval Arab-Islamic world from only one side.
They have treated those achievements as though they existed independently of their own history.

In other words, they have failed to uncover the real and objective, though indirect, relationship between the internal laws governing intellectual development and the broader laws governing the movement of society. As a result, the history of Arab-Islamic thought has remained a closed and static history, almost a history without history, because it has been cut off from its social roots—that is, from its real and objective historical setting.

Only the materialist view of history can uncover this relationship. It allows us to see the heritage in its historical movement, understand the relative value of its different parts, and decide which of them still deserve to remain present in our own time.

Some parts of that heritage still matter because they show a genuine historical connection between the progressive and democratic elements of our cultural past and the progressive and democratic elements of our national culture today.

Yet Arab thinkers and researchers have only very recently begun to bring the materialist view of history into the study of medieval Arab-Islamic thought, whether at the level of theory or in practical research.

Their efforts therefore remain limited. As far as we know, there are only a handful of applied studies. Some offer broad accounts of “scientific thought among the Arabs”. Others deal with particular parts of the philosophical heritage. At the time of writing, we know of only one work that has tried to place the philosophy of this heritage within a complete overall framework.

The theoretical study of the heritage as a general problem is even more limited. On the basis of this same method, we know of only one study that fully meets its requirements and treats the intellectual heritage as a problem for present-day Arab thought, rather than simply as a problem belonging to the past.

That study is a systematic and scientific attempt to uncover “the relationship between thought within the present Arab social structure and the thought that came before it within the previous social structure.”
The present book is another link in this still-new chain of practical attempts.

It is not pure coincidence that these efforts began at roughly the same historical moment. They did not arise simply because a number of individuals happened to become interested in the same question.

They arose from a historical necessity: an objective national need for this kind of systematic and scientific engagement with the intellectual heritage of the Arab peoples at the present stage of their struggle for liberation.

The conditions have now matured for us to solve the problem of the relationship between present-day Arab thought and its inherited past on a new basis—one that fits the revolutionary direction of the Arab liberation movement at this stage in its development.
The attempt to reconsider this heritage is not new. It did not begin only in our own recent period.
The efforts we have just mentioned therefore did not arise in a historical vacuum. They represent a new stage in a problem that began more than a century ago.

It began with a group of Arab thinkers and intellectuals who emerged as pioneers of what came to be called the modern Arab Renaissance, or Nahda. In the field of thought, they expressed—at first spontaneously—the beginnings of an objective loosening in the relationship between Arab feudal social structures and the military-feudal rule of the Turkish Ottoman caliphate.

At the beginning, this loosening was an almost direct effect of the growing crisis known in nineteenth-century international politics as the Eastern Question, which developed as capitalism was moving into its imperialist stage.

The meaning of this term reveals the heart of the matter. It refers to the way the capitalist West of Europe sought to establish imperial control over the countries of the East that made up the greater part of the Ottoman Empire. These were largely the Arab countries.
The European powers exploited the weakness and decline of the Ottoman Empire at a stage when that particular form of feudal relations had historically reached its end.

The “Eastern Question” was therefore one expression of the rivalry between the ambitions of the European imperial powers over the inheritance of the “sick man,” as they then called the Ottoman state—in other words, over access to the East and the Arab countries.

Alongside this weakening of the relationship between Arab social structures and the backward and historically decaying military-feudal rule of the Ottomans, another factor also helped push this group of Arab thinkers and intellectuals toward the ideas that would later be called the Arab Renaissance.
That second factor was their intellectual contact with the social, political, and intellectual movements of nineteenth-century Western Europe.
The Renaissance movement grew and became more clearly defined among Arab intellectuals, army officers, and students, though the two factors we have just described affected them in different ways.

It also developed among the growing commercial bourgeoisie in Lebanon, Egypt, and Syria. Here the driving force was the conflict between the interests of this bourgeoisie and the feudal relations tied to the rule of the collapsing Ottoman Turkish state. This was combined with the bourgeoisie’s desire to link its interests to the capitalist West.
At the same time, the first seeds of national feeling were growing among the Arab masses, together with a desire to free themselves from Ottoman Turkish rule, which had lasted for several centuries.

At first, these feelings appeared as a form of national pride in the achievements of the flourishing periods of medieval Arab civilization. That pride became an early source of awareness of a national existence in the present. Later, it would develop into a force for national liberation.

This change became especially clear after the First World War, as Western imperial powers increasingly moved to impose colonial control over the countries of the East—the Arab countries—in economic, political, military, and cultural forms.

As national feeling among the Arab masses began to take the form of pride in the past, that pride also appeared in literature and other forms of thought as a renewed interest in the different cultural achievements of that past.

At first, however, this return to the heritage took the form of imitating its styles, defending it fanatically, and boasting about it to an extreme degree. People tried to revive its original forms through teaching, publication, and commentary.
In practice, they were often repeating the heritage in a distorted form, without adding to it, developing it, or reconsidering its methods and ideas.

For this reason, the early return to the heritage was backward-looking in its method but progressive in its motives. Its driving force was national resistance to the older colonial challenge of Turkish rule and, later, to the newer challenge of Western imperialism.

After the First World War, the earlier national impulses developed into uprisings and armed national revolutions. The powerful Renaissance movement increasingly became a movement of national liberation with deeper roots among the masses.
At the same time, the movement toward the heritage also began to change.

It was no longer simply a matter of repeating the traditional heritage. It became an attempt to reconsider not only the achievements of that heritage, but also the racist European colonial theories about the heritage of colonized peoples.
Those theories tried to belittle the national history and culture of colonized peoples, cut them off from both, and empty their past of anything that might give them reason to take pride in it.

They also presented these peoples as racially and historically incapable of belonging to the family of peoples able to create civilization or culture—not only in the past, but in the present and future as well.
The move toward this new way of dealing with the heritage was, in itself, progressive.
Yet the practical work carried out in its name was often tied to positions that did not match its progressive aim. In some cases, they directly worked against it.

These positions looked at the heritage from a bourgeois point of view. They took the form of chauvinistic nationalism and stood against a democratic view of culture, both in their understanding of the heritage itself and in their view of its relationship with other cultures.

Internally, the bourgeois approach ignored the social character of the heritage. It stressed its individual side instead, treating it as the work of gifted members of an “elite,” separate from their historical social surroundings and from the human forces of production whose labour created the material basis on which the achievements of the heritage rested.
This bourgeois position also concentrated almost entirely on the visible and finished forms of the heritage.

Externally, it not only tried to ignore the mutual links between the national cultural heritage and other national and world cultures. It also tended to replace European racist theories with new racist theories of its own when judging the national heritage of Asian and African peoples.

One example was the “theory” developed by the ideologues of colonial rule about Black Africans. According to this theory, Black people suffered from biological and creative deficiencies that left them without history and without cultural traditions of their own.
In constructing this “theory,” its authors exploited the fact that historical and colonial conditions had prevented some African peoples from developing a philosophical form of social consciousness.
In connection with this colonial theory, we can recall an observation by the British historian Basil Davidson:

“... The effect of colonial administration proved so overwhelming that many Africans came to believe the slanders directed against their own historical achievements. Inside and outside the continent, Africans accepted—or, out of fear, were forced to accept—the statement of a former governor of Kenya that Africans were so primitive that, in relation to civilization, they were almost like a blank sheet of paper. Yet an important part of the African renaissance in its later years was its rejection and dismissal of this judgment, and its insistence that Africa possessed forms of social thought, organization, and belief that were distinctive and valuable to civilization.”
Another example of a European theory with a racist character appeared in the nineteenth century. It claimed that there were two different ways of thinking: an Eastern way and a Western way.
According to this view, Eastern thought was instinctive and synthetic, while Western thought was logical and analytical.
This racial “theory” appeared in Western bourgeois literature in statements such as the famous line by the English poet: “East is East and West is West, and never the twain shall meet.”
The intellectual imperialism that accompanied European colonial policy in the East also produced another theory of this kind: the theory of Eurocentrism.
In this case, the claim was that philosophy existed only in Europe, and that philosophical thought was centered entirely in that continent.
The bourgeois reaction in the East to such Western racist theories often reproduced the same basic logic. Its answer was racist in character as well.
Under the influence of this reaction, together with other nationalist factors, positions toward the heritage appeared that reflected bourgeois nationalist thought.
We moved from a theory of the “European center of philosophy” to a theory of an “Eastern center”.
The heritage was now viewed in a way that exaggerated both its relative value and the extent of its influence on world and Western cultures and philosophies.

One example can be found in a report presented by the Pakistani philosopher Muhammad Sharif to the Twelfth World Congress of Philosophy. He argued that Islamic philosophy gave humanism its first principles, introduced the West to historical sciences and the scientific method, laid the foundations of the Italian Renaissance, and influenced modern European thought all the way to Immanuel Kant.
There is undoubtedly a historical basis for some of these conclusions.

But when they are presented in such absolute terms, with other historical factors ignored, they become open to scientific criticism. They also take on the character of a new form of bias replacing the rejected bias of the West.
There is another form of this bourgeois nationalist position toward the heritage. It appears in new Salafi or revivalist currents dressed in the language of “modernity.”
Some of these currents introduced the idea of “modernizing” the heritage.
By this they meant interpreting ideas from the past as though they were identical with ideas from the present.

This jumps over every stage of history and ignores the radical changes that took place in inherited ideas over time. It also ignores the economic and social conditions and the scientific discoveries that created ideas in the modern world which could not historically have arisen outside those conditions and discoveries.
We have seen several examples of this kind of “modernization.”
At one time people spoke of “Arab socialism,” and at another of “Islamic socialism”.
Others tried to find “principles of capitalism” in Islam.
Books were written searching for “materialism” in Islamic texts, for “Islamic personalism”, or for “humanism and existentialism in Arab thought”.
